title: Things to Do in Crete When It Rains
seoTitle: Things to Do in Crete When It Rains
seoDescription: Caves, monasteries, museums, wineries, olive mills and cooking classes - the indoor and all-weather options across Crete, and where each one is.
summary: A wet day in Crete is a good day for the parts of the island that have nothing to do with the beach: the caves at Melidoni, Zoniana and Psychro, which are underground and unaffected by weather; monasteries such as Arkadi; the archaeological and folklore museums in Rethymno, Chania and Heraklion; wineries and olive mills, which are working indoor spaces with tastings attached; the pottery workshops at Margarites; and a cooking class, which is the single best use of a wet afternoon. The old towns of Rethymno and Chania also work in rain - the lanes are narrow, roofed cafes are everywhere, and the stone looks better wet. With around 300 sunny days a year, rain is mostly a November-to-March problem, and even then it tends to pass within a few hours.
body:
Crete gets roughly 300 sunny days a year, which is why so many people book here. It still rains - mostly between November and March, occasionally in the shoulder months, and almost never in July or August. When it does, the island has more to offer indoors than most Mediterranean destinations, because so much of what is interesting here was never outdoors to begin with. For the full list of [things to do in Crete](/en/guides/authentic-crete-experiences) in any weather, start there.

## Go underground

Caves are the one category of attraction that does not care what the sky is doing. Crete has thousands, and several are set up for visitors.

- **Melidoni Cave**, in the Rethymno region, is both a natural formation and a memorial - hundreds of villagers sheltering here died during the Ottoman period, and the cave is treated as a monument as much as a geological site.
- **Sfendoni Cave** at Zoniana, on the slopes of Psiloritis, is one of the best-decorated show caves in Greece, with an extensive walkway through stalactite and stalagmite chambers.
- **Psychro Cave** on the Lasithi Plateau, also called the Dikteon Andron, is the cave that mythology names as Zeus's birthplace. It involves a steep walk up and back.

All three are cool and damp regardless of the weather, so the rain outside makes no difference.

## Monasteries and churches

Crete's monasteries are substantial complexes, and most of what you go to see is under a roof or behind a wall. **Arkadi**, about 23 km south-east of Rethymno, is the most significant: a Venetian-facade church, a museum, and a national symbol because of the 1866 explosion during the revolt against Ottoman rule. Rain suits it.

Smaller chapels and monasteries are scattered everywhere and make good morning stops before you decide what the weather is doing.

## Museums and the archaeological sites you can still do

The **Heraklion Archaeological Museum** holds the Minoan collections - the frescoes, the Phaistos Disc, the figurines - and is entirely indoors. It takes two hours minimum and pairs naturally with Knossos, which is open-air but partly roofed, and considerably more pleasant without the summer heat.

Rethymno and Chania both have archaeological and historical-folklore museums that give useful context on the Venetian and Ottoman periods, and both cities have small galleries.

## Wineries and olive mills

Crete produces serious wine and very good olive oil, and visiting a producer is an indoor activity with a tasting attached. There are wineries around Alagni, south of Heraklion, and across the Heraklion wine country, where you can taste indigenous Cretan varieties - vidiano, vilana, kotsifali, liatiko - and see how they are made. Olive mills in the Rethymno region do the same for oil, and the pressing season in late autumn and winter is exactly when the weather is worst, which is convenient.

## Learn to cook

A cooking class is the best possible use of a wet afternoon: it is indoors, it lasts several hours, it ends in a meal, and it gives you something to take home. Most classes on the island start with the garden or the market and finish at a table.

## Craft workshops

**Margarites**, in the Rethymno region, is a working pottery village. The studios are indoors, the kilns are running, and buying directly from the maker is normal. It is a genuinely good rainy-day stop and pairs with Arkadi and Melidoni in a single loop.

## The old towns still work in rain

Rethymno and Chania are both dense enough that rain is manageable. The lanes are narrow, awnings and covered cafes are everywhere, and the Venetian stonework looks better wet than dry. Chania's Venetian harbour is one of the most photographed places in Crete and is arguably more atmospheric under cloud. In Rethymno the Fortezza is exposed, so save that for a clear afternoon and spend the wet hours in the old town instead.

## Or do nothing at all

If you have a villa or an apartment with a view, the correct answer is sometimes to stop. Open a bottle of Cretan wine, put out cheese, olives and bread, and let the afternoon go. The rain usually passes within a few hours, and you go back outside having had the rest you were not going to schedule.

## A loop that works in bad weather

From Rethymno: Arkadi Monastery, then Margarites for pottery and lunch, then Melidoni Cave on the way back. Roughly a half to three-quarter day, almost entirely under cover, and no worse in rain than in sun.

faqs.q: Does it rain much in Crete?
faqs.a: Not in the summer. Crete has around 300 sunny days a year, and rain falls almost entirely between November and March. Even then, showers tend to pass within a few hours rather than settling in for the day.

faqs.q: What can you do in Crete when it rains?
faqs.a: Visit a show cave (Melidoni, Sfendoni at Zoniana or Psychro on the Lasithi Plateau), a monastery such as Arkadi, the archaeological museums in Heraklion, Rethymno or Chania, a winery or olive mill with a tasting, or the pottery workshops at Margarites. A cooking class is the best single option, because it fills the whole afternoon and ends in a meal.

faqs.q: Is Knossos worth visiting in the rain?
faqs.a: It is open-air, so a downpour is unpleasant, but parts of the site are roofed and the crowds thin out considerably. Pairing it with the Heraklion Archaeological Museum - which is fully indoors and holds everything excavated from the site - makes a solid wet-weather day.

faqs.q: Are the caves in Crete open all year?
faqs.a: The main show caves generally operate year-round, though opening hours shorten outside the summer season. They are cool and damp in any weather, so rain outside makes no difference to the visit. Check hours the same morning, since off-season timetables change.

faqs.q: What is there to do indoors in Rethymno specifically?
faqs.a: The old town itself - the lanes are narrow and largely sheltered, and the cafes are covered - plus the archaeological and historical-folklore museums. Just outside town, Arkadi Monastery, the Margarites pottery workshops and Melidoni Cave make a good half-day loop that barely needs an umbrella.
